analysis.one_liner: Bans drug companies from paying generic rivals to delay cheaper copies of their drugs.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to ban "pay for delay" drug settlements was reported favorably by the Judiciary Committee in July 2011 with 9 cosponsors from both parties, but the Senate never brought it to a floor vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a generic drug maker challenges a brand-name drug's patent, the two companies sometimes settle by the brand company paying the generic company to stay off the market for years. The bill would tell the Federal Trade Commission to treat those payments as presumptively unlawful, unless the companies proved with clear evidence the deal actually helped competition. It would also require companies to disclose all related agreements, penalize violators, and strip a generic firm of its 180-day exclusivity reward if it cut an illegal deal.
analysis.who_benefits: People who fill prescriptions, plus the employers, insurers, and government programs that pay for them. Generic versions of brand-name drugs often cost far less, sometimes more than 90 percent off the brand price, so ending settlements that delay generic entry would bring those savings years sooner. The bill's own findings note generics are 67 percent of prescriptions but only 20 percent of drug spending.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Prescription drug buyers and their insurers

how_it_helps.text: Presumes unlawful any settlement in which a generic maker receives anything of value and agrees to delay or limit its own generic drug, unless the companies prove by clear and convincing evidence that the deal's pro-competitive benefits outweigh its anticompetitive effects [S2][S4].
Keeps normal settlements legal: deals where the generic only gets an early launch date, up to $7.5 million for litigation expenses, or a promise not to sue are exempted [S2][S4].

Requires drug companies to file with the FTC any agreements related to a patent settlement within 30 days, with the CEO personally certifying the filing is complete, including oral side deals [S2][S4].
Imposes civil penalties of up to three times the value exchanged and strips a generic maker of its 180-day market exclusivity if a court or the FTC finds its agreement violated the ban [S2][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose payments to generic rivals would become presumptively unlawful and who would face FTC enforcement and penalties, and generic makers who had been accepting those payments in exchange for staying off the market.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name and settled generic drug makers

drawbacks.text: The bill starts from a presumption that any paid settlement is anticompetitive, which would make companies more reluctant to settle patent disputes at all and could mean more drawn-out litigation over drug patents [S4].

Brand and generic companies argued that patent settlements can reflect a fair assessment of litigation risk rather than a scheme to delay competition; the bill answers this with a clear-and-convincing-evidence defense, but companies would bear the burden of proving their deal was actually pro-competitive [S2][S4].
Enforcement is placed solely with the FTC, with a three-year window to bring cases after the settlement is filed, so deals could stand if the FTC declines or fails to act in time [S2][S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large and well documented in the bill's own findings: generics routinely sell at discounts that sometimes exceed 90 percent, and every year a paid settlement keeps one off the market, consumers and public health programs keep paying brand prices. The costs are real but narrower. Legitimate settlements where the generic simply gets an earlier launch date stay exempt, so honest deals were not banned; the main trade-off is more patent litigation and more compliance filings. On balance the bill targeted a practice the findings called more profitable for both drug companies than competition itself, at the direct expense of people paying for the drugs.

outcome.mechanism: The Judiciary Committee approved it unanimously in July 2011 and it was placed on the Senate's calendar of business, where it sat for the rest of the two-year Congress without ever coming up for a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Herb Kohl (D-WI) introduced the bill on January 25, 2011, joined by nine cosponsors including two Republicans, Chuck Grassley and Susan Collins [S1][S5][S6].

The Senate Judiciary Committee ordered it reported favorably on July 21, 2011, and Chairman Patrick Leahy reported it without amendment the next day, placing it on the Senate Legislative Calendar as Calendar No. 110 [S6][S4].
The bill never received a Senate floor vote, and the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, killing it [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers and generic makers that had been sharing the proceeds of delayed competition kept the pay-for-delay tool intact, and prescription drug buyers kept paying brand-name prices for years longer than necessary.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers and paid-off generic rivals

for.name: Sen. Herb Kohl
for.role: U.S. Senator from Wisconsin; bill sponsor and chairman of the Judiciary antitrust subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan group of nine cosponsors.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.role: U.S. Senator from Iowa; senior Republican on the Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan cover from the ranking side of the committee that reviewed it.

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill favorably without amendment and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar as Calendar No. 110.

against.name: Senate
against.role: The chamber where the bill sat on its legislative calendar
against.what_they_did: Never called Calendar No. 110 up for a floor vote at any point in the remaining 17 months of the Congress.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.role: Industry facing civil penalties and a ban on settlement payments to generic rivals
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation restricting drug patent settlements, which the bill's findings described as more profitable for both brand and generic makers than competition.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's ten original supporters included six Democrats, two Republicans, and independent Senator Bernie Sanders, and the Judiciary Committee reported it favorably without amendment, so support crossed party lines even though it never reached a floor vote [S1][S5][S6].

industries.note: The bill would presumptively bar the reverse payments they make to settle patent challenges by keeping generics off the market, with civil penalties up to three times the value exchanged. Their gain from such deals comes directly from delaying discounts that sometimes exceed 90 percent off the brand price [S2][S4].

Generic firms that had accepted payments to stay off the market lose that revenue and could forfeit their 180-day exclusivity for an illegal deal. Generic firms that compete rather than settle gain, because more low-cost copies would reach the market sooner [S2][S4].

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: They pay a large share of the roughly $235 billion in annual U.S. prescription drug spending, so earlier generic entry cuts their costs along with patients' [S4].
